title: Dynamic prefix-aware batcher with KV reservation policy for mixed-length dialogs
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: In mixed prompt/response workloads we observe pathological tail latency and KV cache thrashing when long prefixes (>=1024 tokens) interleave with short, low-latency requests. The existing continuous batcher tries to maximize packing efficiency but has no mechanism to reserve KV cache slots or adapt the batching window based on predicted continuation lengths. That leads to frequent KV evictions, fragmented GPU memory, and repeated re-warm of KV caches which increases p99 latency for large-context requests and raises unit token cost.
proposal: Implement a prefix-aware continuous batcher variant that: 1) classifies incoming requests by estimated remaining tokens (short | medium | long) using fast heuristics on prompt metadata / token count; 2) reserves a small fraction of KV cache capacity (configurable per-GPU pool) for active long-context slots to avoid eviction during bursts of short requests; 3) dynamically adjusts batching window and slot allocation when a long context is actively streaming tokens to prioritize KV residency for that slot; 4) opportunistically serializes cold KV slabs to host memory (PCIe) for underused slots instead of full eviction; 5) exposes runtime knobs and telemetry to quantify reservation hit-rate, eviction thrash, and memory fragmentation.
design_decisions:
- Reservation is quota-based (percentage of GPU cache bytes) rather than fixed slot count to handle variable kv size across models.
- Classification must be fast and conservative: rely on token_count_hint when present, otherwise use median historical length per route for quick estimate.
- During reservation, short requests are allowed to co-exist but are de-prioritized for hot-swap to avoid preempting currently reserved long-context slots.
- Serialization to host uses pinned page pool and an async background worker so token path isn't blocked; restore happens on first token of the resumed request.
- Safety: reservation is a soft guarantee—if GPU memory pressure becomes critical (>95%), reservation can be temporarily evicted by OOM policy with telemetry alerting.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Microbenchmarks: For synthetic mixed workload (30% long >=2048 tokens, 70% short <=64) the p99 end-to-end latency for long requests decreases by >=15% vs baseline continuous batcher with same throughput.
2) GPU memory fragmentation metric decreases (measured by free-block-count) or at least eviction-thrash reduces by >=30%.
3) Cache hit-rate for 'long' class improves by >=25% while overall throughput (tokens/s) changes by <=3% negative.
4) Unit tests for reservation logic, classification, and host-serialization exist and pass in CI.
5) Telemetry: new dashboard panels for reservation utilization, serialized-slabs count, and reservation-preemptions are created and visible in Console canary.
6) Feature flag gating present with runtime knobs exposed in Dedicated and Private deployments.
7) Documentation: design doc and runtime config guide published in Confluence and Console settings annotated.
8) Canary: rolled out to 1% of traffic for hosted then 10% after 72h if no regressions.

experiments_and_results:
Experiment: Synthetic mixed workload (30% long >=2048, 70% short <=64) running on 4x A100s. Baseline: continuous-batcher-v1. New variant: prefix-reservation-v1 with 12% KV quota reserved. Runs: 6x 1-hour trials. Results: 
- Long request p99: baseline 1,860ms -> 1,525ms (18% improvement).
- Long request p95: baseline 980ms -> 840ms (14% improvement).
- Overall tokens/s: baseline 122k -> variant 119k (-2.4%).
- Eviction-thrash (evictions per minute): baseline 420 -> variant 245 (-41.7%).
- Serialized slab restores: avg 3.2 restores/hour per GPU.
- Observed downside: small increase in short-request p95 by ~40ms in highest util runs due to slightly longer scheduling decision path.
Conclusion: net win for mixed workloads important to enterprise customers; trade-off acceptable when knobbed per-pool.
risks_and_mitigation:
- Risk: Reservation can reduce peak throughput in purely short workloads. Mitigation: per-pool defaults = 0 reservation and auto-tune based on observed distribution; enable only for pools with >=X% long-context traffic.
- Risk: Host serialization latency spike on restore. Mitigation: limit serialization to slabs that haven't been accessed for T seconds and keep small hot-resident cache.
- Risk: Complexity increases maintenance cost. Mitigation: keep codepaths feature-flagged and documented; add comprehensive metrics so we can disable quickly if regressions observed.
